title: Iranian Attacks Surge in Strait of Hormuz as Tehran Battles Blockade and Loss of Leverage
snippet: Attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz have hit peak levels since the U.S.-Iran war began, as Tehran seeks to regain control over the strategic waterway amid plummeting oil revenues.
content:
Attacks on commercial shipping in the critical Strait of Hormuz have surged to their highest levels since the U.S.-Iran war erupted early this year, according to newly released maritime data. The escalation comes as Tehran attempts to re-exert influence over the strategic waterway while grappling with a severe U.S. naval blockade and falling global crude prices.

Data compiled from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reveals that reported attacks exceeded 30 in October—the highest monthly total since hostilities broke out in late February. The trend has spilled into November, with at least 22 incidents already logged across the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz, and the Gulf of Oman. Prior to October, reported incidents averaged about 10 per month.

Economic Strain Drives Tehran's Escalation

The Strait of Hormuz, which handled nearly 20% of global oil shipments before the conflict, has turned into a contested battleground. In response to initial U.S. and Israeli military strikes, Iran attempted to choke off maritime traffic. Washington countered by imposing a strict blockade on Iranian ports, severely curtailing Tehran’s crude exports.

According to maritime tracking firm Kpler, Iranian oil stored on water outside the U.S. blockade zone dropped to zero this month following final offloads in China. Analysts warn that Iran’s oil revenues could effectively dry up by mid-December, driving Tehran to step up attacks in a desperate bid to force concessions from Washington.

Trump Rejects Diplomatic Deals

Despite the escalating clashes, President Donald Trump signaled no interest in diplomatic compromise, stating on Truth Social that the U.S. "doesn't need a deal with Iran." Trump asserted that Washington holds both Iranian financial assets and strategic control over the waterway, while indicating he would not hesitate to launch additional military strikes if necessary.

Meanwhile, energy markets have experienced a slight reprieve as non-Iranian Gulf exporters find alternative transit methods. However, Hamidreza Azizi, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, warned that market stability remains fragile. "Markets appear to be increasingly assuming that a return to full-scale war is unlikely and that oil supplies will gradually recover," Azizi said. "But that assumption could change quickly if Iran decides to intensify the confrontation."

Recent Tanker Strikes Highlight Ongoing Threat

The ongoing risk to commercial shipping was highlighted over the weekend when three tankers—the Marshall Islands-flagged Captain Leon and Hong Kong-flagged vessels Torkel and Arina—were hit by strikes while exiting the strait near Oman. Maritime risk consultancy Marisks noted that Iranian involvement was "assessed as likely," warning that the vital southern shipping corridor remains under severe threat.
